title: Bidirectional BFS in Barcelona: Meeting in the Middle ⚡
description: Watch a real-map grid route in Barcelona where two BFS searches launch from start and goal at the same time. When their frontiers meet, the path is reconstructed—often cutting the explored area dramatically.
ig_caption:
Bidirectional BFS: Why Meeting in the Middle Cuts Search Space in Half — launch two searches and meet in the middle ⚡

In standard BFS, you expand layer-by-layer from the start until you hit the goal. Bidirectional BFS runs two BFS processes simultaneously: one from the start, one from the goal, each expanding outward. Instead of exploring the entire “blast radius” from only one side, the combined search depth is effectively about half, so the visited nodes can drop from roughly O(b^d) toward O(b^(d/2)) in typical graphs (b = branching factor, d = distance).

On this Barcelona (Eixample) grid visualization:
1) BFS-Side expands from the starting intersection.
2) BFS-Tail expands from the destination intersection.
3) The moment any node appears in both visited sets, you’ve found the connection.
4) Reconstruct the full route by stitching parents from each side.

Takeaway: If you only need a shortest path in an unweighted graph, Bidirectional BFS is a powerful graph optimization—especially when start and goal are far apart.

Debate question: When would a single BFS be simpler (or even faster) than meeting-in-the-middle?
